# CS3101: Empirical Benchmarking and Experimental Evaluation

**Project**: Infinite Dungeon  
**Course**: CS3101 — Design and Analysis of Algorithms  
**Dataset**: generated by the headless suite [`benchmark_runner.py`](benchmark_runner.py)  
**Output data**: [`benchmark_results.csv`](benchmark_results.csv) (3,822 records)  

To reproduce every number below:
```bash
python benchmark_runner.py
```
Sections 6–8 can be re-run on their own (they replace only their own rows in the CSV):
```bash
python benchmark_runner.py --only locks,negative,danger
```

---

## 1. Experimental Methodology

- **Environment**: Python 3.12.8, pygame-ce 2.5.8, Windows 11 (64-bit).
- **Timing**: `time.perf_counter()`. In experiments 1 and 3 the timed call also runs under `tracemalloc` (to measure peak memory), which inflates absolute times by roughly 2–4× — compare times *within* a table, not across machines.
- **Memory**: `tracemalloc` peak allocation in KB.
- **Input equivalence**: within each experiment every algorithm gets the identical grid, start and goal.
- **Seeds**: pathfinding floors use seeds 101, 202, 303, 404, 505; generators seeds 1–10; chase queries floors 1–30 with `random.Random(7)`; knapsack `Random(42)`; vaults `Random(2026)`; locks and negative weights floors 1–50 of each generator (placement `Random(seed)`); danger map floors 1–30.
- **Optimality reference**: Dijkstra's terrain-weighted path cost.

---

## 2. Pathfinding

### 2.1 Spawn → Exit on Whole Floors (Rooms + MST)

| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 20×20 | BFS | 0.490 | 53.0 | 9.40 *(steps)* | 6.94 | — |
| 20×20 | Dijkstra | 0.510 | 57.8 | 11.06 | 6.28 | 1.000 |
| 20×20 | **A\*** | 0.503 | **21.4** | **11.06** | 6.25 | **1.000** |
| 20×20 | Greedy Best-First | 0.257 | 12.8 | 12.12 | 5.74 | 1.092 |
| 35×35 | BFS | 3.541 | 319.2 | 29.00 *(steps)* | 29.14 | — |
| 35×35 | Dijkstra | 7.688 | 320.6 | 33.88 | 25.44 | 1.000 |
| 35×35 | **A\*** | 5.089 | **153.6** | **33.88** | 24.18 | **1.000** |

| 50×50 | BFS | 3.962 | 427.8 | 53.00 *(steps)* | 47.16 | — |
| 50×50 | Dijkstra | 8.042 | 433.6 | 58.51 | 51.92 | 1.000 |
| 50×50 | **A\*** | 5.543 | **258.6** | **58.51** | 33.09 | **1.000** |
| 50×50 | Greedy Best-First | 1.041 | 80.2 | 63.61 | 19.81 | 1.090 |

*BFS reports its cost as the number of steps (it does not know about weights), so its cost column is not comparable; its real terrain cost is measured in §2.2.*

### 2.2 Enemy Chase Queries (what each enemy type solves every turn)

600 queries on 30 different 35×35 floors, enemy 4–12 steps from the player. Path costs are all re-measured with the real terrain weights.

| Algorithm (enemy) | Avg nodes expanded | Avg time (ms) | Avg path cost | Cost / optimal | Optimal paths |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| BFS (slime) | 81.2 | 0.239 | 10.87 | 1.050 | 77.2 % |
| Greedy Best-First (goblin) | **10.2** | **0.058** | 11.24 | 1.079 | 60.3 % |
| **A\* (skeleton)** | 20.6 | 0.113 | **10.34** | **1.000** | **100 %** |
| Dijkstra (flying beast) | 87.9 | 0.368 | **10.34** | **1.000** | **100 %** |

*In the game the flying beast runs Dijkstra with all terrain treated as cost 1 (it flies over mud); here it runs on the normal weights so it can serve as the optimality reference.*

### 2.3 Interpretation

1. **A\* vs Dijkstra — same answer, less work.** A\* returned exactly Dijkstra's cost in every whole-floor run and in all 600 chases, while expanding 2.7× (20×20), 2.1× (35×35) and 1.7× (50×50) fewer nodes on whole floors and **4.3× fewer** on chase-length queries. That is admissibility (§4.4 of ALGORITHMS.md) in practice: the heuristic prunes without ever costing optimality. The advantage is largest on short queries, where the straight-line estimate is close to the true distance.
2. **Greedy Best-First is fast but wrong a lot.** It expanded half as many nodes as A\* in chases (4× fewer on whole 35×35 floors), but only 60 % of its paths were optimal, and on average they cost 8 % more (18 % more on whole 35×35 floors). Ignoring $g(n)$ is exactly what makes it both cheap and unreliable — which is why the goblin uses it.
3. **BFS is only optimal when weights don't matter.** It found the cheapest route 77 % of the time: whenever a mud pool lay on the step-shortest path, it walked through and paid for it (+5 % cost on average). In game, slimes visibly get stuck in mud while skeletons go around.
4. **Memory** follows explored nodes: A\* and Greedy keep smaller frontiers than Dijkstra and BFS.

## 3. Procedural Dungeon Generation

| Grid | Generator | Avg time (ms) | Floor coverage | Avg dead ends | Avg spawn→exit (steps) | Valid |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 25×25 | Recursive Backtracking | 14.39 | 60.1 % | 7.3 | 18.4 | 100 % |
| 25×25 | Rooms + MST (Kruskal) | 7.82 | 22.9 % | 1.0 | 22.9 | 100 % |
| 35×35 | Recursive Backtracking | 23.81 | 56.8 % | 15.8 | 27.6 | 100 % |
| 35×35 | Rooms + MST (Kruskal) | 13.55 | 28.5 % | 0.7 | 30.3 | 100 % |
| 50×50 | Recursive Backtracking | 128.67 | 53.8 % | 34.5 | 38.0 | 100 % |
| 50×50 | Rooms + MST (Kruskal) | 32.24 | 17.7 % | 0.2 | 52.9 | 100 % |

*Times include `tracemalloc` overhead and the full pipeline (pillars, mud pools, repair, two BFS sweeps, metrics).*

### 3.1 Interpretation

1. **Shape**: the maze generator fills 54–60 % of the map with tight corridors and many dead ends; MST floors are 18–29 % open rooms joined by corridors, with almost no dead ends because 20 % of rejected edges are added back as loops.
2. **Scaling**: the maze generator is $O(W \cdot H)$ and its time grows with area (×9 from 25×25 to 50×50); the MST generator's room phase depends on the number of rooms, so it grows more slowly. Generation runs once per floor change, behind the fade-in, so a few tens of milliseconds is not noticeable in play.
3. **Every floor is valid**: one connected component and a reachable exit, every seed, every size.
4. **Spawn → exit distance (double-sweep BFS)**: in a separate in-game audit (30 floors per generator, 35×35), the average distance on MST floors rose from **16 steps** (old rule: first room → last room) to **31** (minimum 7 → 26). The farthest walkable tile averaged 34 steps on MST floors and 40 on maze floors (where the farthest tiles are dead ends, not rooms).

### 3.2 Entity Placement Audit (in game, 60 floors)

| Problem | Before | After |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Enemies / items spawned inside pillars | ≈ 4 % | 0 |
| Enemies within 4 steps of the player's spawn | ≈ 20 % | 0 (minimum 6) |
| Items on stairs or stacked | yes | 0 |

## 4. 0/1 Knapsack: Dynamic Programming vs Greedy

### 4.1 Random Instances (weights 1–15, values 5–100)

| Items ($N$) | Capacity ($W$) | DP value | Greedy value | Greedy ratio | DP time (ms) | Greedy time (ms) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 10 | 20 | 330 | 330 | 100.0 % | 0.307 | 0.064 |
| 10 | 50 | 445 | 445 | 100.0 % | 0.939 | 0.084 |
| 10 | 100 | 472 | 472 | 100.0 % | 1.377 | 0.062 |
| 25 | 20 | 428 | 426 | 99.5 % | 0.722 | 0.096 |
| 25 | 50 | 685 | 685 | 100.0 % | 2.472 | 0.085 |
| 25 | 100 | 972 | 972 | 100.0 % | 5.838 | 0.095 |
| 50 | 20 | 585 | 585 | 100.0 % | 1.481 | 0.269 |
| 50 | 50 | 1040 | 1035 | 99.5 % | 4.780 | 0.117 |
| 50 | 100 | 1505 | 1497 | 99.5 % | 10.848 | 0.147 |
| 100 | 20 | 858 | 858 | 100.0 % | 3.531 | 0.523 |
| 100 | 50 | 1424 | 1424 | 100.0 % | 12.576 | 0.194 |
| 100 | 100 | 2102 | 2102 | 100.0 % | 24.958 | 0.219 |

### 4.2 Realistic Treasure Vaults (the instances the player actually faces)

1,000 vaults generated exactly as the game does (relics until their total weight ≥ 1.7 × capacity, 6–10 relics), capacity 24 (a new knight):

| Metric | Result |
| :--- | :---: |
| Vaults where greedy is sub-optimal | **550 / 1000 (55.0 %)** |
| Average greedy ratio | 96.97 % |
| Worst greedy ratio | 77.0 % |
| Average gold lost when greedy fails | 5.6 |
| Average DP time | 0.123 ms |
| Average greedy time | 0.023 ms |

### 4.3 Interpretation

1. **Pseudo-polynomial DP**: runtime grows with the table size $N \times W$ — 231 cells take ~0.3 ms, 10,201 cells ~25 ms. Greedy stays near-constant because sorting $N \le 100$ items is trivial.
2. **Random instances hide greedy's weakness**: with many small items and loose capacity, greedy reaches 99.5–100 %. The gaps appear when capacity is tight relative to item weights.
3. **Vaults are designed to be tight**: few items (6–10), weights up to 10, capacity 24. Here greedy is wrong **more than half the time** and can leave almost a quarter of the gold behind, while the DP still answers in about a tenth of a millisecond. This is why the planner shows both, and why the vault is sized at 1.7× capacity.

## 6. Locked Doors & Keys

35×35 floors, seeds 1–50 per generator, up to 3 locks each. "Solvable" requires Kahn's order to exist, its replay to succeed, *and* an independent flood-fill simulation to open every lock and reach the exit.

| Generator | Cut vertices | Locks placed | of which room seals | Exit locked | Tarjan | Whole plan | Solvable |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Rooms + MST | 2.5 | 2.90 | 2.34 | 86 % | 6.70 ms | 73.7 ms | 100 % |
| Recursive Backtracking | 27.2 | 1.36 | 0 | 0 % | 15.37 ms | 74.9 ms | 100 % |

### 6.1 Interpretation

1. **Cut vertices alone are not enough on room floors**: there are only ≈ 2.5 per floor and few cut off a useful region. Treating a lock as a vertex cut (room seals) gives almost the full 3 locks per floor and locks the exit on 86 % of floors.
2. **Maze floors are the opposite**: plenty of cut vertices (27 per floor) but most cut off short dead ends (< 8 tiles), and maze chambers have too many entrances to seal, so locks guard side branches and the exit is never locked.
3. **Correctness**: every plan was solvable and no lock was ever dropped by the replay check. The cost (≈ 75 ms, mostly the pairwise BFS for dependency edges) is paid once per floor, behind the fade-in.

---

## 7. Negative Edge Weights: Bellman–Ford vs Dijkstra

Same 100 floors, each with 2 locks (closed), 2 shrines and 3 rifts placed exactly as in game; distances measured from the spawn.

| Generator | V | E | BF passes | BF time | Dijkstra time | Dijkstra wrong (floors) | Wrong tiles when wrong | Worst error | Floors with a sealed rift |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Rooms + MST | 343 | 1,884 | 13.6 | 8.68 ms | 0.62 ms | 18 % | 15.6 | 3 turns | 46 % |
| Recursive Backtracking | 692 | 2,929 | 26.7 | 34.12 ms | 1.95 ms | 48 % | 55.5 | 6 turns | 20 % |

36 of 300 rifts (12 %) closed a negative cycle and were sealed (25 / 150 on room floors, 11 / 150 on mazes).

### 7.1 Interpretation

1. **Dijkstra's failure is real, not theoretical**: on the graphs the planner actually uses, it returns wrong distances on a fifth of room floors and half of maze floors, by up to 6 turns.
2. **Early exit makes Bellman–Ford practical**: about 14–27 passes instead of $V - 1$, i.e. ≈ 25× less work than the worst case. It is still ≈ 15× slower than Dijkstra, which is the price of handling negative weights; at under 35 ms it runs on each right-click without a hitch.
3. **Negative cycles occur naturally**: random rift exits sometimes land within $R - 1$ steps of the entrance. Detecting them from a virtual source and sealing the rift keeps every planner query well-defined (the unit tests re-run Bellman–Ford from a virtual source after sealing and find no negative cycle).

---

## 8. Danger Map: One Multi-Source Search vs k Searches

30 room floors (35×35); $k$ enemies at random walkable tiles; walking-enemy model (mud = 3).

| Enemies $k$ | Multi-source nodes | Multi-source time | $k$ separate: nodes | $k$ separate: time | Speed-up | Identical |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 4 | 349 | 3.85 ms | 1,396 | 14.85 ms | 3.9× | 100 % |
| 8 | 349 | 3.43 ms | 2,792 | 29.05 ms | 8.5× | 100 % |
| 16 | 349 | 3.75 ms | 5,583 | 58.98 ms | 15.7× | 100 % |

### 8.1 Interpretation

The multi-source search settles every walkable tile exactly once whatever $k$ is, so its cost is flat, while $k$ separate searches scale linearly in $k$. The two answers matched on every tile of every instance.

---

## 9. Summary

1. **A\*** matches Dijkstra's optimal cost on every test while expanding 1.7–4.3× fewer nodes.
2. **Greedy Best-First** is the cheapest search (about half of A\*'s nodes in chases) but optimal only 60 % of the time — the price of ignoring path cost.
3. **BFS** is optimal only when terrain weights don't matter (77 % of chases).
4. **Both generators** produce 100 % valid, connected floors; the double-sweep BFS doubles the average spawn → exit distance on MST floors.
5. **Knapsack DP** beats greedy in 55 % of realistic vaults at a cost of ~0.1 ms.
6. **Locks** are 100 % solvable; vertex cuts (room seals) are what let room floors lock the exit (86 % of floors).
7. **Bellman–Ford** is ≈ 15× slower than Dijkstra but always right; textbook Dijkstra is wrong on 18–48 % of floors once shrines and rifts add negative edges, and 12 % of rifts had to be sealed because they formed negative cycles.
8. **Multi-source Dijkstra** answers "nearest enemy" for every tile in one search: 15.7× faster than 16 separate searches.
